Counsel: Sarath Jayamanne, P.C. with Dinindu Rathnayake, Anjuna Wilwaraarachchie, Himalshi Fernando and Uvindu Bandara for the 1st Accused-Appellant. JUDGMENT AMAL RANARAJA, J.
1. The accused-appellants (hereinafter referred to as the appellants have
been indicted in the High Court of Colombo along with two others, in
case number HC-3076/2006. The charges in the indictment are as
follows;
01. That on or about the period between July 13, 2005, and July 14,
2005, at Peliyagoda, in the district of Colombo, within the
jurisdiction of this court, the appellants wrongfully confined
Hettiarachchige Abeysiri alias Ranjith; thereby committed an
offence punishable in terms of Section 339 read with Section 32
of the Penal Code.
02. On or around the 14th of July, 2005, in the location and course
of action of the above first charge, you, as the above named third
accused, has aided and abetted the above first and second
accused, to commit said offence in the first charge, and as a
result, they have committed said offence; thereby you have
committed an offence punishable under Section 339 read with
Section 102 of the Penal Code of Sri Lanka.
03. On or around the 14th of July, 2005, in the location and course
of action of the above first charge, you, as the above named
fourth accused, has aided and abetted the above first and second
accused, to commit said offence in the first charge, and as a
result, they have committed said offence; thereby you have
committed an offence punishable under Section 339 read with
Section 102 of the Penal Code of Sri Lanka.
04. That on or about July 14, 2005, during the same course of
transaction as above, the first and second accused caused
mental/physical pain to Hettiarachchige Abeysiri alias Ranjith, to
obtain a confession/statement; thereby committed an offence
punishable in terms of section 2(4) of the Convention Against
Torture, and Other Cruel, Inhuman, or Degrading Treatment or
Punishment Act No. 22 of 1994.
05. In the time, place, the location, and course of action of the above
fourth charge, you, as the above named third accused, has aided
and abetted the above first and second accused, to commit said
offence in the fourth charge, and as a result, they have committed
said offence; thereby you have committed an offence punishable
under Section 2(4) read with Section 2(2)(b) of the Convention
Against Torture, and Other Cruel, Inhuman, or Degrading
Treatment or Punishment Act No. 22 of 1994.
06. In the time, place, the location, and course of action of the above
fourth charge, you, as the above named fourth accused, has
aided and abetted the above first and second accused, to commit
said offence in the fourth charge, and as a result, they have
committed said offence; thereby you have committed an offence
punishable under Section 2(4) read with Section 2(2)(b) of the
Convention Against Torture, and Other Cruel, Inhuman, or
Degrading Treatment or Punishment Act No. 22 of 1994.
07. During the same course of transaction as the first charge above,
the first and second accused committed murder by causing the
death of Hettiarachchige Abeysiri alias Ranjith; thereby
committed an offence punishable in terms of section 296 of the
Penal Code.
2. At the conclusion of the trial, the learned High Court Judge has
convicted the appellants of the first, fourth and the seventh charges and
sentenced them as follows;
Two years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 15,000.00
with a term of 6 months simple imprisonment in default, in
respect of the first charge.
Ten years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.50,000.00 with
a term of 1 year simple imprisonment in default, in respect of the
fourth charge.
The appellants have been sentenced to death in respect of the
seventh charge.
Also, the appellants have been ordered to pay a sum of
Rs.1,000,000.00 (one million) each as compensation with a term
of 2 years simple imprisonment in default.
Case of the Prosecution
3. During the period in question, the appellants being police officers have
been assigned to the crimes branch of the Peliyagoda Police Station. On
July 13th, 2005, the deceased named in the seventh charge has been
arrested on suspicion of stealing a telephone from PW04 and has been
brought to the Police Station’s crime branch.
4. The officers on duty at that time being the appellants, have been
informed of this incident by PW04. Following this the appellants have
detained the deceased and begun an investigation. It is alleged that the
deceased was held by the appellants improperly resulting in wrongful
restraint. Furthermore, it is claimed that the appellants subjected the
deceased to physical and mental pain with the intention of obtaining a
confession or statement. These physical assaults are further alleged to
have caused injuries that ultimately lead to the deceased’s death.
Case of the Appellants
5. The appellants have asserted that they investigated a complaint
regarding the theft of a telephone. During this investigation, that they
detained both the deceased and PW01 intending to produce them before
a Magistrate within twenty four hours of their detention. Unfortunately,
the deceased has fallen ill during this period and has subsequently
passed away. The appellants have denied the incidents referred to in
the first, fourth and seventh charges.
Grounds of Appeal
6. When the matter was taken up for argument, the learned counsel
appearing on behalf of the appellants raised the following grounds of
appeal;
I. The learned High Court Judge has failed to properly consider the
legal requirements of section 294(3) of the penal code of Sri Lanka
II. PW01 and pw08 contradict each other but the learned High Court
Judge has not considered the material interse contradictions.
III. The prosecution has failed to exclude a criminality of third
parties.
IV. Has the learned High Court Judge wrongly rejected the evidence
of PW08?
V. Has the learned High Court Judge wrongly evaluated the evidence
of PW01?
VI. Has the learned High Court Judge prejudged the case in
contravention of section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure
Act No. 15 of 1979?
VII. Has the learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate the medical
evidence properly?

7. Accordingly, the learned High Court Judge has concluded that the
bodily injury inflicted upon the deceased was, in the ordinary course of
nature, sufficient to cause the death of the deceased. Consequently, the
appellants have been convicted of murder under the third limb of
Section 294 of the Penal Code of Sri Lanka.
8. The third limb of the Section 294 of the Penal Code provides as follows;
“ 294. Except in the cases hereinafter excepted, culpable homicide is
murder-
Thirdly - If it is done with the intention of causing bodily injury
to any person, and the bodily injury intended to be in>licted is
suf>icient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.”
9. The third limb to Section 294 of the Penal Code of Sri Lanka states that
culpable homicide amounts to murder, if the act is done with the
intention of causing bodily injury to any person, and the bodily injury
intended to be inflicted is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to
cause death.
10. The offender must deliberately intend to inflict a specific bodily harm or
injury to a person. Unlike the first limb, the prosecution does not need
to prove that the accused had a specific conscious intent to cause
death. The injury that the offender intended to inflict must be
objectively fatal, meaning it is serious enough to cause death in the
ordinary natural course of events.
11. In the case of Vithana and Another Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka [2007]
1 SLR 169, Sisira de Abrew J. held as follows,
“The ingredients that must be proved by the prosecution in order to prove
a charge of murder under the 3rd limb of section 294 are that:
(i) The accused in>licted a bodily injury on the victim.
(ii) The victim died as a result of the above bodily injury.
(iii) The accused had the intention to cause the bodily injury.
(iv) The above injury was suf>icient to cause the death of the victim in
the ordinary course of nature.”
12. “Sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature” is a critical
element to distinguish murder from culpable homicide. A Court is a
legal expert, not a medical one. Therefore, it relies heavily on the
testimony and reports of the forensic pathologist or medical officer who
conducted the postmortem examination.
13. The doctor’s opinion is relevant in this instance, and the prosecution
should explicitly ask the medical expert during examination, “Was this
injury sufficient to cause death in the ordinary cause of nature?”. A
court can thereafter evaluate medical details regarding the depth, width
and the location of the injury. Injuries to vital organs are almost always
ruled as naturally sufficient to cause death. The court would also look
at the capacity of the weapon to cause lethal damage.
14. Dr. M.P.A.B Abeysinghe, an assistant Judicial Medical Officer in
Colombo has conducted the post-mortem examination of the deceased.
The postmortem report has been submitted as evidence and marked
15. In his testimony, Dr. Abeysinghe has identified both external and
internal injuries on the deceased. He has concluded that some internal
injuries correspond with the external injuries, while others did not. He
has categorised certain injuries as non-grievous and others grievous.
Ultimately, he has opined that the death has resulted from
haemorrhagic shock, caused by multiple muscle injuries sustained
from blunt weapon trauma.
16. Although Dr. Abeysinghe has testified as previously mentioned, he has
not elaborated on whether any of those injuries were sufficient to cause
death in the ordinary course of nature. He has merely stated the
following regarding the 9th internal injury;

19. That is, the appellants did have a “murderous intention”, when they
allegedly assaulted the deceased. As discussed earlier in the judgement
the mental element that needs to be established regarding the third
limb of Section 294 of the Penal Code of Sri Lanka, is that an accused
intended to cause such bodily injury to the deceased. The learned High
Court Judge’s conclusion is, therefore, inconsistent with this
requirement. Hence, the learned High Court Judge has misdirected
himself on the facts and the relevant legal principles discussed above.
20. With regard to the alleged assault by the appellants on the deceased,
the prosecution has relied on the testimonies of PW01 and PW08. PW01
has been detained with the deceased on suspicion of stealing a phone,
while PW08 was at the material time a female police officer attached to
the crime branch of the Peliyagoda Police Station. PW01 and PW08 have
testified as follows;

22. That is, PW08 had been on duty at the crime branch that morning when
the second appellant bought the deceased to that location. The second
appellant has then seated the deceased on a chair and questioned him
regarding the incident for which he has been detained. PW08 has
observed the deceased being questioned in that manner for
approximately ten minutes. Afterward she had gone to the canteen to
have her breakfast. When she returned to her seat, she has noticed that
the deceased appeared to be in discomfort and had rested his head
against the wall. PW08 has then informed the acting Headquarters
inspector of the police station (PW21) about her observations.
23. Considering the previously mentioned testimonies of PW01 and PW08,
it becomes evident that there are material discrepancies between their
testimony. The discrepancies highlight several inconsistencies. These
include the simultaneous presence of both appellants at the crime
branch, whether the deceased was assaulted by the appellants, the
presence of PW01 to observe any potential assault of the deceased, and
the atmosphere at the crime branch at that specific time, specifically if
other individuals were present who might have impeded an assault.
24. The inconsistencies and contradictions interse in the testimonies of
PW01 and PW08 undermine their credibility. These discrepancies
suggest that their narratives may not be reliable, casting doubt on the
validity of their testimony. It is important to examine these
inconsistencies closely, as they play a significant role in assessing the
overall trustworthiness of the evidence presented.
25. To overcome this impediment, the learned High Court Judge has
disbelieved the testimony of PW08. The judge has stated that PW08’s
testimony was disregarded because she had testified under stressful
circumstances.
26. PW08 has testified on two occasions. That is, on September 14th, 2011,
and June 28th, 2018. On September 14th, 2011, evidence in chief has
been presented, cross examination conducted, and the witness has
been released after re-examination. Subsequently, following an
application made on behalf of the second appellant, PW08 has been
recalled solely for cross examination on June 28th, 2018. During this
latter appearance, the witness’s attention has been directed to certain
photographs, and she has been questioned about the setting of the
crime branch in the Peliyagoda Police Station.
27. At that time, almost seven years later, PW08 has stated that she was
grappling with an issue and felt depressed under those circumstances;

28. PW08 has not stated that she was in a depressed state when she
testified on September 14th, 2011. However, the learned High Court
Judge has stated in the disputed judgement that PW08 was in a
significantly impaired state when she testified entirely, which has not
been the case. Therefore, the learned High Court Judge has rejected
PW08’s evidence on unfounded grounds representing a misdirection of
facts.
29. Furthermore, if the deceased had been handcuffed to a window grill and
subsequently assaulted, the movement of his hand likely would have
caused injuries in the wrist area. However, Dr. Abeysinghe has observed
no such injuries. The same lack of injuries applies to the soles of the
deceased’s feet, where no injuries were found either. Therefore, these
circumstances do not medically corroborate the testimony of PW01.
The testimony lead on behalf of the prosecution also indicates that the
deceased had attempted to escape from PW04 (the complainant of the
theft of a telephone) when he was taken to his lodging. A third individual
has apparently pursued and apprehended the deceased, subsequently,
returning him to PW04. During this pursuit, PW04 has lost sight of the
deceased. Upon the deceased’s return, a fresh injury near the nose has
been observed. This suggests the possibility that the deceased
sustained injury due to an assault by the third individual during that
incident. If other injuries were sustained at that time, they would not
have been visible to PW04 or PW12, the duty officer at the Paliyagoda
Police Station because, the deceased was dressed in a sarong and shirt
when brough to the police station by PW04. Moreover, the prosecution
has not presented any testimony regarding the age of the injuries
inflicted on the deceased nor the pain caused by the injuries nor, the
deceased’s ability or inability in normal activities despite being injured.
Therefore, the fact that the deceased had not exhibited major discomfort
after the incident, cannot rule out the possibility that the injuries were
caused by such third person.
30. The statement “contents of a document has to be established by
producing such document” reflects the best evidence rule in law,
meaning a document’s written contents must be proved by submitting
the actual document itself rather than relying on someone’s spoken
memory or descriptions. The law prefers primary evidence, which is the
original document produced to a Court for legal inspection.
31. In the case of Keerthi Bandara vs. The Attorney General [2000] 2 SLR
245, Niinian Jayasuriya J., has held as follows;
“The best evidence rule which is a fundamental tenet in the law of
evidence would totally exclude the oral evidence of a police of>icer in
regard to the contents of a matter which is required by law and which in
fact has been reduced to writing, to be led after refreshing his mind from
the document without the document being marked.”
32. The prosecution, through the testimony of PW21, who was the acting
headquarters inspector of the particular police station at the time of the
alleged incidents, has attempted to orally establish specific regulations.
These regulations concern an officer’s attire when on duty, and the
procedure to be followed when a suspect is brought to a police station
and detained. The prosecution has attempted to further assert that the
appellants violated these regulations, thereby making them guilty of
unlawful restraint of the deceased.
33. The regulations referenced must be documented adequately and it is
essential for the prosecution to produce the actual document
containing those regulations. Unfortunately, the prosecution has failed
to provide this necessary evidence. Furthermore, they have not offered
any explanation for this omission.
34. In cases where Court favours primary evidence, such as the original
document, containing the relevant regulations it becomes imperative for
the documents to be presented for legal scrutiny. Consequently, any
testimony provided by PW21, as previously mentioned, should be
disregarded and considered invalid. Without the primary evidence the
testimony lacks sufficient credibility to support the prosecution’s case.
35. Section 283 of Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 15 of 1979 provides
as follows;
“283. The following provisions shall apply to the judgments of courts
other than the Supreme Court or Court of Appeal:
(1) The judgment shall be written by the Judge who heard the

case and shall be dated and signed by him in open court at the time of pronouncing it, and in case where appeal lies shall contain the point or points for determination, the decision thereon, and the reasons for the decision. (2) It shall specify the offence if any of which and the section of
the law under which the accused is convicted and the punishment to which he is sentenced.
(3) If it be a Judgment of acquittal it shall state the offence of
which the accused is acquitted.
(4) When a judgment has been so signed it cannot be altered or
reviewed by the court which gives such judgment: Provided that a clerical error may be recti>ied at any time and that any other error may be recti>ied at any time before the court rises for the day.
(5) The judgement shall be explained to the accused affected
thereby and a copy thereof shall be given to him without delay if he applies for it.
(6) The original shall be >iled with the record of proceedings.

(Sections 279 and 283 shall apply to every judgement of a Primary Court-See section 33(2) of the Primary Courts’Procedure Act.) 36. Accordingly, in giving reasons for the decision, a Court is required to
appreciate the testimony of witnesses in its entirety and in the context
of the evidence as a whole, rather than evaluate piecemeal. Isolated
statements should not be detached from their context. Discrepancies
should be assessed according to their materiality and their effect on the
overall credibility of their account.
37. In the case of James Silva Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka (1980) 2 SLR
167, Rodrigo J., has stated as follows;
“A satisfactory way to arrive at a verdict of guilt or innocence is to
consider all the matters before the Court adduced whether by the
prosecution or by the defence in its totality without
compartmentalising and, ask himself whether as a prudent man, in the
circumstances of the particular case, he believes the accused guilty of
the charge or not guilty.”
38. Further in the case Dayarathne Wijesinudera and Two Others vs. The
Attorney General (CA/HCC/29-30/2015) decided on 13.02.2020,
Achala Wengappuli J.,
“The superior Courts have consistently laid emphasis on the duty to
consider the evidence as a whole, irrespective of whether the trial was
held before a jury or Judge. In The King v Appuhamy 37 NLR 281, it is
stated that "One has to look at the whole case". A similar approach was
adopted by the Court of Criminal Appeal in King v Buckley 43 NLR 474,
which imposed a duty on the jurors that they should view the evidence
as a whole.”
39. With regard to the judgement under challenge, it appears that the
learned High Court Judge has assessed the witnesses’ testimony
piecemeal, rather than in its entirety and considered isolated
statements out of context. Further, the learned High Court Judge
appears to have concluded that the offences charged against the
appellants have been proved beyond a reasonable doubt, before
evaluating whether the testimony established the essential ingredients
of those offences. In doing so, the learned High Court Judge appears to
have prejudged the issue and thereby misdirected himself.
40. In those circumstances, I am inclined to interfere with the conviction,
disputed judgement, together with the sentencing order and proceed to
set aside the same.
41. I acquit the appellants of the charges but make no order regarding
costs.
Appeal allowed.
